title: Bombay High Court Lets Gadkari Sue Meta, X, Google Over AI Deepfakes
excerpt: The civil suit over fabricated videos linking the Union minister to the E20 fuel programme could become a landmark test of platform liability and personality rights in India.
body:
• The Bombay High Court has permitted Union Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari to file a civil suit against Meta, X Corp, Google and YouTube over AI-generated deepfake videos and defamatory content.
  • Gadkari alleges unknown persons used AI to fabricate videos falsely linking him and his family to financial gains from the E20 fuel programme, which he says is run by the Petroleum Ministry.
  • The case revives the debate over safe harbour protections for tech platforms under Section 79 of India's IT Act and could set a precedent for handling AI deepfakes targeting public figures.
  • The government amended IT rules in February 2026 requiring platforms to act within three hours of receiving orders to remove unlawful AI-generated content.

The Bombay High Court on Monday allowed Union Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari to institute a civil suit against Meta Platforms, X Corp, Google LLC and YouTube over the alleged circulation of AI-generated deepfake videos and defamatory social media content. Justice Abhay Ahuja granted leave under Clause XII of the Letters Patent, a procedural step required when part of the cause of action falls outside the court's territorial jurisdiction.

Gadkari, represented by advocate Sandeep S. Ladda, argued that the disputed content was accessible to users in Maharashtra, giving the Bombay High Court grounds to hear the case. The court will take up his application for interim relief, including a temporary injunction to remove the content, at a later date.

What the Suit Alleges

The proposed suit claims that unidentified individuals circulated AI-generated videos, social media posts and reels that falsely portrayed Gadkari as personally responsible for the government's E20 fuel programme — a blend of 20 per cent ethanol and 80 per cent petrol. Some content allegedly claimed that he and his family had financially benefited from the policy.

https://x.com/LawBeatInd/status/2081967888613990688

Gadkari maintains he has no role in the programme. The ethanol-blending initiative, he argues, is administered exclusively by the Union Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.

According to the suit, the fabricated content used AI-generated versions of Gadkari's name, image, likeness, facial features and voice without his consent, causing what the plea describes as "grave and irreparable" harm to his reputation, goodwill and personality rights, according to Inc42.

"The purpose and object of filing the suit is not to curtail or prevent the public at large from engaging in discussion, debate, analysis or fair, just and bona fide criticism of any decision taken by the plaintiff himself or by his office."

— From Gadkari's plea, as reported by Madhyamam Online

Platform Liability and Safe Harbour Under Scrutiny

Besides Meta, X Corp, Google and YouTube, the suit names the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) as respondents. Unidentified content creators have been listed as John Doe defendants.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=8_j4-DJzj58

The case has revived a long-running debate over safe harbour — the legal shield under Section 79 of India's Information Technology Act that protects platforms from liability for content posted by users. The government amended the IT Rules in February 2026 to require platforms to proactively identify and label synthetically generated information and to act within three hours of receiving a court or government order to remove unlawful content, according to Outlook Business. Failure to comply could cost platforms their safe harbour immunity.

Legal analysts have argued that platforms are no longer passive hosts. With proprietary AI systems such as X's Grok that can generate content, tech companies increasingly resemble content originators rather than neutral intermediaries. As one legal analysis by DSK Legal noted, "intermediary immunity in the AI era is increasingly conditional and may not readily extend to platforms that actively generate and amplify unlawful content," Outlook Business reported.

A Broader Pattern of AI Misuse

Gadkari's suit arrives amid a wave of deepfake-related legal actions. Union minister Piyush Goyal filed a police complaint last week alleging that his remarks outside Parliament were maliciously altered using AI and circulated as a deepfake, according to Inc42. Separately, Nagpur Cyber Police registered a criminal case earlier this month against four online content creators — associated with the accounts of Manish Kashyap, Desi Boys NCR, Harshit Rathi and Anklesh Invate — over videos about Gadkari and E20 that allegedly contained false and misleading statements.

The E20 rollout itself has generated political friction. A group calling itself the E20 Janta Party has demanded that consumers be given the option of unblended petrol and has called for Gadkari's resignation — despite the petroleum ministry being responsible for the programme. Aam Aadmi Party's Arvind Kejriwal has announced a national town hall on the issue at the Constitution Club of India on August 1, and an online petition seeking access to unblended petrol has gathered nearly 200,000 signatures, according to Outlook Business.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad — many of whom consume Indian political content primarily through social media — the case raises questions about the reliability of viral videos and posts that shape perceptions of Indian policymakers. The outcome will signal how effectively Indian courts can compel global platforms to act against AI-generated disinformation, a challenge not limited to any one country.

What Happens Next

The court has yet to schedule hearings on Gadkari's application for interim relief. The government, meanwhile, is drafting the Digital India Act, which is expected to overhaul existing safe harbour provisions and impose clearer obligations on platforms to moderate AI-generated content. The Gadkari suit — combining questions of deepfake technology, platform accountability, personality rights and political speech — could end up shaping the terms of that debate.
nri_angle: The case will test whether Indian courts can compel global tech platforms to act against AI-generated disinformation — a precedent relevant to diaspora members who rely on social media for news about Indian politics.
